title: Quicksort & Partitioning Schemes
summary: The in-place divide-and-conquer sort built around picking a pivot and partitioning around it — and the two classic partition schemes, Lomuto and Hoare, that implement that idea.

slides.markdown:
Quicksort's idea: pick an element as the **pivot**, rearrange the array so everything smaller than the pivot ends up to its left and everything larger ends up to its right — the pivot is now in its final sorted position — then recursively quicksort the two sides.

Unlike [merge-sort](merge-sort), which always splits at the midpoint and merges after recursing, quicksort does its real work **before** recursing, during the partition, and needs no extra array to do it — it rearranges in place. That's why quicksort usually wins on raw speed: no allocation, better cache locality, less data movement.

The price: where you split depends entirely on the pivot you pick and the data around it, which is the source of quicksort's O(n²) worst case and the reason pivot choice is most of this topic.

slides.sectionTitle: The Lomuto partition scheme, step by step
slides.markdown:
Lomuto's scheme fixes the **last element** as the pivot and walks the rest of the array with two indices: `i` marks the boundary of "elements confirmed smaller than the pivot so far," and `j` scans forward.

For each `j` from the start to the second-to-last element: if `arr[j]` is less than the pivot, increment `i` and swap `arr[i]` with `arr[j]` — this grows the "smaller than pivot" region by one. Once `j` has scanned the whole array, swap the pivot (still at the last position) into `arr[i + 1]`, its correct final spot.

After this pass, everything at or before index `i + 1` is ≤ pivot, everything after is > pivot, and `i + 1` is returned as the pivot's final index — the split point for the two recursive calls.

Lomuto is popular for teaching because the two-index logic is easy to state precisely, at the cost of doing somewhat more swaps than Hoare's scheme (next).

```python
def quicksort_lomuto(arr, lo, hi):
    if lo < hi:
        p = lomuto_partition(arr, lo, hi)
        quicksort_lomuto(arr, lo, p - 1)
        quicksort_lomuto(arr, p + 1, hi)

def lomuto_partition(arr, lo, hi):
    pivot = arr[hi]          # last element is the pivot
    i = lo - 1                # boundary of "< pivot" region
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if arr[j] < pivot:
            i += 1
            arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
    arr[i + 1], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[i + 1]
    return i + 1               # pivot's final index
```

The partition returns the pivot's final resting index, and the two recursive calls exclude it — it's already in its correct place and never needs to move again.

slides.sectionTitle: The Hoare partition scheme — why it does fewer swaps
slides.markdown:
Hoare's original scheme, usually taught with the **first element** as pivot, uses two pointers starting at opposite ends and walking inward. The left pointer advances while its element is less than the pivot; the right pointer retreats while its element is greater. When both stop, if the pointers haven't crossed, swap the two elements they point to (each is on the "wrong" side) and continue.

When the pointers cross, the partition is done — but here's the key difference from Lomuto: **the pivot is not necessarily at the returned index**, and the split isn't "everything ≤ pivot then everything > pivot" — it's "everything ≤ pivot in the left region, everything ≥ pivot in the right region," with the pivot value somewhere inside one of them.

Because Hoare only swaps when an element is provably on the wrong side (never swaps an element already correctly placed with itself), it does roughly **3x fewer swaps** than Lomuto on average — real, measurable speed on large arrays.

slides.sectionTitle: Lomuto vs Hoare partitioning the same array — where the pointers end up
slides.markdown:
Run both schemes on the same small array and compare where things land.

<<< Image: the array [5, 3, 8, 4, 2, 7, 1, 6] shown twice side by side; left side labelled "Lomuto" with pivot=6 (last element) highlighted, index i and j shown mid-scan with the growing "< pivot" region shaded, ending with 6 swapped into its final index; right side labelled "Hoare" with pivot=5 (first element) highlighted, two pointers starting from opposite ends and moving inward with swap arrows drawn only where elements are out of place, ending with the crossing point j marked and the pivot value NOT necessarily at index j >>>

The visual point to take away: Lomuto ends with the pivot sitting exactly at the returned index. Hoare ends with a valid partition boundary at the returned index, but the pivot's value can be anywhere in either half — a detail that trips people up when they try to reason about Hoare the same way they reason about Lomuto.

slides.sectionTitle: Picking a pivot: first/last element, median-of-three, or random
slides.markdown:
The partition scheme is only half the story — where you split, and therefore how balanced the recursion is, depends entirely on which element you crown pivot. Four common choices:

- **First or last element.** Trivial to implement, but catastrophic on already-sorted or reverse-sorted input (next slide).
- **Median-of-three** (first, middle, last — take the median of those three). Cheap, and specifically defeats the sorted/reverse-sorted worst case, though adversarial inputs can still be constructed against it if the attacker knows the scheme.
- **Random element.** Pick uniformly at random and swap it into the pivot position before partitioning. No fixed input can be adversarial against it (next-next slide).
- **Median-of-medians.** A real O(n) algorithm that guarantees a good pivot every time, giving worst-case O(n log n) quicksort — almost never used in practice because its constant factor is too large to be worth it.

Random pivot selection is the practical default in production quicksort implementations.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a sorted (or reverse-sorted) input triggers the O(n²) worst case
slides.markdown:
Take the naive "pivot = last element" scheme on an already-sorted array. Every partition puts the pivot — the largest element in the current range — at the very end of its final position, meaning the split is **1 element vs n − 1 elements**, every single time.

That gives a recursion of depth n instead of log n, with each level doing O(n) partition work: total cost is `n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1` = **O(n²)**. The same failure happens in reverse for reverse-sorted input with a first-element pivot.

This is the textbook worst case, and it's worth internalizing that it isn't a rare edge case — sorted or nearly-sorted data shows up constantly in practice (re-sorting an already-sorted log, appending to a sorted structure), which is exactly why naive fixed-position pivots are considered a real bug, not just a theoretical concern.

slides.sectionTitle: Randomized pivots: turning a worst case into an astronomically unlikely one
slides.markdown:
Randomizing the pivot doesn't eliminate the O(n²) worst case — it's still mathematically possible — it makes the *specific input* that triggers it unknowable in advance and its *probability* vanishingly small.

Here's the reasoning: with a uniformly random pivot, the **expected** running time is O(n log n) for *any* fixed input, because on average a random element lands somewhere in the middle third of the sorted order often enough that the recursion stays balanced. The probability of hitting the true worst case — always picking the min or max, every single recursive call — shrinks exponentially with n; for any array of meaningful size it's effectively zero.

This is why production sort implementations don't bother with median-of-medians (guaranteed O(n log n), large constant): random pivots get the same practical guarantee — "this will not happen" — far more cheaply. It's also why an adversary who doesn't know your random seed cannot construct an input to attack a randomized quicksort, unlike a fixed-pivot one.

slides.sectionTitle: Lomuto vs Hoare — swap count, duplicate handling, index semantics
slides.markdown:
| | Lomuto | Hoare |
|---|---|---|
| Pivot position after partition | Exactly at the returned index | Not necessarily — pivot value can be anywhere in either half |
| Swap count | More (swaps on every "< pivot" find) | Fewer (~3x less on average) |
| All-duplicate input | Degrades to O(n²) — every element compares equal, pivot never moves | Handles duplicates well, splits roughly evenly |
| Recursive call bounds | `[lo, p-1]`, `[p+1, hi]` | `[lo, p]`, `[p+1, hi]` — includes p on the left |
| Typical use | Teaching, simpler to prove correct | Production-grade implementations |

The duplicate-handling row is the one people miss: an array of all-equal elements is a genuine worst case for naive Lomuto, while Hoare's opposite-ends approach naturally splits it close to evenly.

slides.sectionTitle: Recursing on the smaller half first to cap recursion depth at O(log n)
slides.markdown:
Even with a good pivot strategy, naive recursion — always recurse left then right — can blow the call stack on a skewed-but-not-worst-case split, because the *deeper* branch of recursion determines the stack depth, and nothing forces you to recurse into the smaller side first.

The fix: after partitioning, **compare the two side lengths and recurse into the smaller one first** (or, equivalently, use a loop for the larger side and only truly recurse for the smaller one — "tail-call" the big side). Since the smaller side is at most half the current range, this guarantees the recursion depth is **O(log n)** regardless of how uneven any individual split is.

This is a real production concern, not academic: without it, a language without tail-call optimization can stack-overflow on a large adversarial-shaped input even when the randomized-pivot average case is fine — because the *depth* bound and the *average time* bound are different guarantees.

slides.sectionTitle: Mixing Lomuto-style logic with a Hoare-style partition index
slides.markdown:
The single most common quicksort bug: implementing Hoare's partition but then recursing with Lomuto's call bounds — `quicksort(lo, p-1)` and `quicksort(p+1, hi)` — instead of Hoare's `quicksort(lo, p)` and `quicksort(p+1, hi)`.

Why it breaks: Hoare's returned index `p` is a **partition boundary**, not the pivot's final resting place — the element at index `p` might not even be the pivot value, and it might still need to move during the left recursive call. Excluding it with `p - 1` can drop that element from being sorted at all, or cause **infinite recursion** in the specific case where the partition puts everything into one side (`p == hi`, and `quicksort(lo, hi)` gets called again unchanged).

The fix is mechanical, not a deep insight: Hoare's bounds are always `[lo, p]` and `[p+1, hi]`. If you can't remember which scheme you copied, check whether your partition function assigns the pivot into its own final slot (Lomuto) or just returns a boundary (Hoare) — that tells you which recursive bounds to use.

slides.sectionTitle: Trusting a fixed first-element pivot without guarding against sorted input
slides.markdown:
Writing quicksort with `pivot = arr[0]` (or `arr[-1]`) and no further thought is the fastest way to pass a small test case and then time out on a large one — many coding-interview judges specifically include a sorted or reverse-sorted array as a test, precisely to catch this.

The fix is one line, not a rewrite: before partitioning, swap a **randomly chosen** element (or a median-of-three) into the pivot position, then run the exact same fixed-position partition logic unchanged. You don't need a different partition scheme — you need the input to the scheme to no longer be adversarial.

Say this explicitly in an interview if you write a fixed-pivot quicksort under time pressure: "I'm using a fixed pivot for simplicity here; in production I'd randomize it or use median-of-three to avoid the O(n²) sorted-input case." That one sentence signals you know the failure mode exists, even if you don't have time to code the fix.
